q: This iconic white marble mausoleum was built by a Mughal emperor for his beloved wife. Which monument is this?
fact: The Taj Mahal was commissioned by Shah Jahan in 1632 in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal.
points: Built between 1632–1653 in Agra, on the bank of the Yamuna river
Combines Persian, Islamic, and Indian architectural styles
Designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983

q: Which emperor renounced violence after the brutal Kalinga War and spread Buddhism across Asia?
fact: Ashoka's transformation after Kalinga is one of history's most documented moral conversions.
points: Fought and won the Kalinga War around 261 BCE, then renounced further conquest
Adopted and promoted Buddhism, sending missionaries across Asia
His edicts on rocks and pillars survive today; the Lion Capital is India's national emblem

q: Which empire was the first to unify nearly the entire Indian subcontinent under one rule?
fact: The Maurya Empire, founded by Chandragupta Maurya around 321 BCE, was the subcontinent's first major unifying power.
points: Founded c. 321 BCE with guidance from the strategist Chanakya
Reached its largest extent under Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE
Administered through a sophisticated bureaucracy described in the Arthashastra

q: Who led India's independence movement through non-violent civil disobedience?
fact: Gandhi's philosophy of Satyagraha became the defining strategy of the independence movement.
points: Pioneered Satyagraha — non-violent resistance — starting in South Africa and continuing in India
Led major campaigns: Non-Cooperation (1920), Salt March (1930), Quit India (1942)
Assassinated in January 1948, months after Independence

q: This massive red sandstone fort in Delhi was the main residence of Mughal emperors. What is it called?
fact: The Red Fort served as the principal Mughal residence in Delhi for nearly 200 years.
points: Built by Shah Jahan starting in 1638 as his new capital's centerpiece
Served as the seat of Mughal power until 1857
India's Prime Minister hoists the national flag here every Independence Day

q: Which 1757 battle, won partly through betrayal, marked the start of British dominance in Bengal?
fact: Robert Clive's secret alliance with Mir Jafar decided the outcome before the battle truly began.
points: Fought on 23 June 1757 between the East India Company and Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah
Mir Jafar's defection left the Nawab's larger army leaderless mid-battle
Gave the Company control of Bengal's treasury — the seed of colonial rule

q: Which Maratha leader is famous for his guerrilla warfare tactics against the Mughals?
fact: Shivaji built a network of mountain forts and pioneered hit-and-run tactics that frustrated much larger Mughal armies.
points: Founded the Maratha Kingdom and was crowned Chhatrapati in 1674
Used Ganimi Kava (guerrilla warfare) suited to the rugged Sahyadri terrain
Built or captured over 300 forts to secure Maratha territory

q: This massive temple in Tamil Nadu was built by Rajaraja Chola I and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. What is it called?
fact: The Brihadeeswarar Temple at Thanjavur is considered an engineering marvel of the 11th century.
points: Completed around 1010 CE, dedicated to Lord Shiva
Its vimana (tower) rises about 66 metres, capped by a single granite block
Part of the UNESCO-listed 'Great Living Chola Temples'

q: Which South Indian empire's capital, Hampi, was once one of the wealthiest cities in the world?
fact: Under Krishnadevaraya, Vijayanagara's capital Hampi rivaled the great cities of Europe in wealth and scale.
points: Founded in 1336; reached its peak under Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509–1529)
Hampi's bazaars reportedly traded in diamonds by the bagful, per foreign travelers
Fell after the Battle of Talikota in 1565, and the city was sacked and abandoned

q: Which Mughal emperor pursued religious tolerance and married into Rajput royal families?
fact: Akbar's policy of inclusion, including abolishing the jizya tax, helped stabilize a vast, diverse empire.
points: Abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims and promoted Din-i Ilahi, a syncretic court philosophy
Formed marriage alliances with Rajput houses, including Jodha Bai
Reorganized administration through the mansabdari system

q: In which year did the catastrophic Third Battle of Panipat shatter Maratha momentum?
fact: The 1761 defeat against Ahmad Shah Abdali's forces set back Maratha expansion by a generation.
points: Fought on 14 January 1761 between the Marathas and Ahmad Shah Abdali's Afghan-led coalition
Months of attrition and cut supply lines weakened the Marathas before the final clash
Tens of thousands died, opening a power vacuum the British later exploited

q: Who is traditionally credited as the author of the Arthashastra, the treatise that guided Chandragupta Maurya's rise?
fact: Chanakya (also known as Kautilya) is considered one of history's earliest political strategists.
points: Also known as Kautilya; served as advisor and mentor to Chandragupta Maurya
The Arthashastra covers statecraft, economics, military strategy, and law
Often compared to Machiavelli, though written roughly 1,800 years earlier

q: Which ancient university, destroyed in 1193 CE, was one of the world's first great residential centers of learning?
fact: Nalanda drew scholars from across Asia for nearly eight centuries before its destruction.
points: Founded around the 5th century CE in present-day Bihar
At its peak housed thousands of students and teachers from across Asia
Destroyed by Bakhtiyar Khilji's forces in 1193, ending centuries of scholarship there

q: Which dynasty's naval expeditions briefly extended Indian influence into Southeast Asia under Rajendra Chola I?
fact: Rajendra Chola I's naval campaigns reached as far as the Srivijaya kingdom in maritime Southeast Asia.
points: Rajendra Chola I (r. 1014–1044) built one of the era's most powerful navies
Campaigns reached the Srivijaya empire across the Bay of Bengal and Malacca Strait
The Cholas are unusual among Indian dynasties for sustained overseas military reach

q: Which Mughal emperor's death in 1707 triggered the empire's long terminal decline?
fact: Aurangzeb expanded the empire to its largest extent but left it overstretched and fiscally strained at his death.
points: Ruled from 1658 to 1707, the longest reign among the major Mughal emperors
Pushed the empire to its greatest territorial extent, but at huge military cost
War of succession and regional revolts accelerated decline after his death

q: Which freedom fighter's famous last words before execution were 'Inquilab Zindabad'?
fact: Bhagat Singh was executed in 1931 at age 23, becoming a lasting symbol of revolutionary resistance.
points: Executed on 23 March 1931 along with Rajguru and Sukhdev
Associated with the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association
'Inquilab Zindabad' ('Long live the revolution') became a lasting rallying cry

q: In the ancient Battle of the Ten Kings described in the Rigveda, which king led the victorious Bharata tribe?
fact: This semi-legendary battle, fought along the Ravi river, is one of the earliest recorded conflicts in Indian tradition.
points: Described in the Rigveda (Mandala 7), among the oldest surviving Indian texts
King Sudas of the Bharata tribe defeated a confederation of ten rival kings
Fought along the Ravi river (ancient Parushni) in present-day Punjab region

q: The Lion Capital atop Ashoka's pillar at Sarnath was later adopted as independent India's national emblem. How many lions does it depict facing outward?
fact: Four lions stand back-to-back, though only three are visible from any single viewing angle.
points: Erected by Ashoka at Sarnath around the 3rd century BCE
Originally topped with a wheel (chakra), fragments of which survive
Adopted as India's State Emblem in 1950; the Ashoka Chakra also appears on the national flag

q: Which Gupta-era mathematician is credited with foundational work related to the concept of zero and place-value notation?
fact: Aryabhata's 5th-century work laid crucial groundwork later built upon by Brahmagupta and others.
points: Wrote the Aryabhatiya around 499 CE, covering mathematics and astronomy
Worked with place-value notation and accurate approximations of pi
Correctly proposed that Earth rotates on its axis, well ahead of his time

q: Which 18th-century ruler of Mysore, known as the 'Tiger of Mysore,' died defending his capital against the British in 1799?
fact: Tipu Sultan died at the siege of Seringapatam, becoming a lasting symbol of resistance to British expansion.
points: Son of Hyder Ali; ruled Mysore from 1782 until his death in 1799
Pioneered early war rockets used against British forces
Died defending Seringapatam during the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War

q: Which ISRO mission made India the first country to land near the Moon's south pole in 2023?
fact: Chandrayaan-3's Vikram lander touched down on 23 August 2023, a date now marked as National Space Day.
points: Launched 14 July 2023 from Sriharikota
Landed near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023
Made ISRO the first space agency to land in that specific region

q: Which South Indian dynasty was famous for building a powerful navy that campaigned across the Bay of Bengal?
fact: Rajendra Chola I's naval campaigns reached as far as Srivijaya in modern Indonesia and Malaysia.
points: Reached its peak under Rajaraja Chola I and Rajendra Chola I
Built the Brihadeeswarar Temple at Thanjavur
One of the few pre-modern Indian states to run an overseas naval empire

q: Which self-taught Indian mathematician's notebooks astonished Cambridge professor G.H. Hardy in the early 20th century?
fact: Ramanujan produced thousands of original results in number theory with almost no formal training.
points: Born in Tamil Nadu in 1887, largely self-taught in advanced mathematics
Corresponded with G.H. Hardy at Cambridge starting in 1913
His 'lost notebook' is still yielding new mathematical insights today

q: Which 1999 conflict was fought to dislodge infiltrators from high-altitude posts in the Kashmir region?
fact: Fighting at peaks like Tiger Hill, above 16,000 feet, made Kargil one of the highest-altitude wars in history.
points: Fought in the Kargil district of Kashmir in 1999
Indian forces recaptured strategic peaks including Tiger Hill
Ended with a return to the pre-conflict Line of Control

q: Which queen of Gondwana chose to take her own life rather than be captured after being wounded in battle against a Mughal general in 1564?
fact: Durgavati personally led her army against Akbar's forces in present-day Madhya Pradesh.
points: Ruled the kingdom of Garha-Katanga as a widowed regent
Fought Akbar's general Asaf Khan in 1564
Took her own life with her dagger after being wounded, rather than be captured

q: Which dynasty's queen, Rudrama Devi, ruled in her own right in the 13th century — a rarity for the era?
fact: Rudrama Devi ruled the Kakatiya kingdom of present-day Telangana for nearly three decades.
points: Succeeded her father Ganapati Deva around 1262 CE
Personally led military campaigns to defend her kingdom
One of very few women to rule a major Indian dynasty in her own name

q: Which 1741 naval battle saw an Indian kingdom decisively defeat a Dutch East India Company fleet — a rare Asian victory over a European colonial navy?
fact: Travancore's victory under Marthanda Varma ended serious Dutch ambitions on India's southwest coast.
points: Fought near Colachel on the Travancore coast in 1741
Travancore's forces under Marthanda Varma defeated the Dutch fleet
One of the first total defeats of a European navy by an Asian power

q: Which Vijayanagara emperor's earliest surviving inscription is dated to 26 July 1509, the same day tradition holds his coronation took place?
fact: Krishnadevaraya's coronation is traditionally linked to Krishna Janmashtami, the birthday of the god he was named for.
points: Third ruler of the Tuluva dynasty, reigned 1509–1529
Defeated the Bijapur Sultanate early in his reign at the Battle of Diwani
Patronized the Telugu 'Ashtadiggajas' — eight celebrated court poets
